speaker: Karina Nguyen
title: The Agent Reasoning Interface: Claude, ChatGPT Canvas, Tasks, Operator — with Karina Nguyen
question: In AI product development, how does a team actually use evaluations to move from a prompted prototype to a post-trained model?
guest: Everything starts with a prompted baseline prototype. Then we craft specific evaluations to capture the behaviors we care about and measure progress with the model. We make sure the evals are good, and crucially, make sure that the prompted baseline actually fails on those evals, because then you have something to hill-climb on. Once you start iterating on model training, it's still very iterative. Every time you train the model and look at your evals going up, that's good. But you also want to make sure the model is not super overfitting to those evals, and that's where you run it on other evals like general intelligence benchmarks to check for regressions.

points.core: Every new feature starts as a prompted baseline before any model training begins.
points.note: Accept: prototyping with a prompted base model first to establish a behavioral baseline before investing in fine-tuning or RL. Do not credit: generic mentions of building an MVP.

points.core: Task evaluations must be hard enough that the prompted baseline actually fails them.
points.note: Accept: designing evals where the prompted baseline leaves clear headroom so post-training has a measurable gradient to hill-climb on. Do not credit: merely saying 'write good evals' without specifying baseline failure or headroom.

points.core: Teams run general intelligence benchmarks alongside task evaluations to catch post-training overfitting.
points.note: Accept: tracking broad capability or regression suites during iterative training to ensure feature-specific gains do not degrade core model performance. Do not credit: generic mentions of testing for bugs.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Evaluations act as the fixed yardstick that makes each step of that transition a measurable decision rather than a guess.

A team starts by prototyping with prompts on a strong general model, then reads real outputs and does error analysis to learn how the product actually fails. Those failure modes become an eval suite: a curated set of representative and adversarial inputs, with graders (code checks, human-calibrated LLM judges, or expert review) that encode what "good" means. The prompted prototype's score on that suite becomes the baseline.

From there, the team iterates on prompts, retrieval and tooling until gains plateau. The remaining gap, such as persistent failure categories, cost, or latency, is the justification for post-training. The same error analysis tells them what training data to collect or synthesize, and often the graders themselves are reused to filter data or as reward signals.

The fine-tuned model is then run against a held-out split of the same evals, compared directly with the prompted baseline, and checked for regressions. After launch, production failures feed back into the suite, so it keeps guarding against drift.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Teams start by logging real traffic from their prompted prototype and conducting error analysis to turn recurring failures into a golden evaluation suite of deterministic assertions and human-calibrated LLM-as-a-judge rubrics. Initially, these evals guide prompt engineering and establish baselines for quality, latency, and cost. Once prompting hits a ceiling—failing to fix systematic errors or requiring prompts too bloated and expensive for production—evaluations transition from passive scorecards into active post-training machinery.

While strictly holding out the golden test set to prevent contamination, teams reuse their automated graders to filter production traces and synthetic teacher-model outputs into clean datasets for supervised fine-tuning, distilling cumbersome instructions directly into model weights. Those same programmatic checks and rubrics also score multiple candidate generations to construct preference pairs for DPO or supply verifiable reward signals for reinforcement learning. Finally, the held-out eval suite gates deployment, verifying that the smaller, faster post-trained model matches or beats the prompted baseline without hidden regressions before new production failures seed the next training cycle.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Evals guide the whole path. Each stage tells you whether the next, more expensive step is worth taking.

A team usually starts by prompting a strong base model and running it on real tasks. Then it reads the failures closely and sorts them into categories such as wrong format, hallucinated facts, bad tool calls, or the wrong tone. Those categories become the eval suite. The checks include code assertions, LLM-as-judge rubrics checked against human labels, and a golden set reviewed by experts.

Next the team improves the prompt, retrieval and tooling until the scores stop rising. If a few failure types stay stuck, or cost, latency or consistency matter more, that's the evidence for post-training. Logged failures and corrected outputs become supervised fine-tuning data. The graders, or a reward model trained on preference data, can provide the signal for RLHF, DPO or reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

Before shipping, the fine-tuned model is compared with the prompted baseline on held-out evals. Those include checks for regressions on general abilities and safety, and checks that the model isn't gaming the reward. Production monitoring then finds new failures, which go back into the eval suite.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The team first turns the prompted prototype into a baseline. It collects representative user tasks and known failure cases, defines what a good answer looks like, and scores the prototype. Those results show which failures can be fixed with a prompt or product change and which are persistent enough to target with post-training.

For those persistent failures, the team creates training examples that demonstrate the desired behavior, or pairs of answers that show which response is preferred. It keeps a separate set of evaluation cases out of training. After each training run, it compares the candidate with the prompted baseline on those held-out cases, checking whether the targeted failures improved and whether existing capabilities regressed. The comparison should also reflect how the model will ship, including its prompt and tools.

If the candidate misses the bar, the team inspects the failures, adjusts the training data, and reruns the comparison. Once the candidate meets the release criteria, production feedback supplies new cases for the next round.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A team starts by defining what a good answer looks like for its product. It gathers realistic inputs, including cases where the prompted prototype fails, and writes checks or scoring guidelines that reflect what users care about. It then evaluates the prototype to establish a baseline and tries prompt changes against the same criteria.

If important failures persist, the team uses those patterns to guide post-training. For example, if a support assistant keeps promising refunds outside policy, the team can train it on separate examples of policy-correct replies or on pairs of replies labeled to show which is better. It keeps a representative set of cases out of both training and prompt tuning for a fair comparison.

The team then compares the post-trained model with the prompted baseline on those held-out cases. It checks whether the targeted failures fell, whether other tasks got worse, and whether the gains justify the cost. After deployment, new failures become evaluation cases for the next round.
